title: Detection of Determine Physical Locations
summary: This strategy detects reconnaissance aimed at determining the physical locations of the victim organisation, ATT&CK sub technique T1591.001. An adversary collects addresses of offices, data centres and executive residences from public sources, mapping services, property records and social media, then uses that knowledge for facility surveillance, courier and delivery social engineering, or physical intrusion. The telemetry that makes it detectable sits in three places: web proxy and secure web gateway logs showing searches that pair the organisation name with address, map or direction terms, recursive domain name system resolver logs showing lookups for mapping and geolocation services, and physical access control or visitor management records that reveal someone probing a site. The signal is weak on its own, so the rule depends on context such as an external source address, an unusual account, or a repeated pattern across several sites in a short time. The strategy fails when staff and marketing teams search their own office locations constantly, and when proxy logs do not resolve the true client behind a shared egress address.

beginner.definition: Before an attack, someone may want to know where your buildings are. They look up your office addresses, your data centre sites and the homes of senior staff. This detection looks for searches that combine your company name with address or map words. It turns that quiet research into an alert your team can review.
beginner.whyItMatters: Knowing where you are is useful in ways that pure network attacks are not. A parcel can be sent to a specific office and reception desk. A person can stand outside a side door with a clipboard and a plausible story. A named executive address can support blackmail or intimidation. These risks are hard to see from inside the network, so awareness of the research stage is the advantage. It also helps the physical security team move before anything happens.
howItWorks: Your web proxy records each web request, including the site and the search terms in the address.
The rule keeps requests to mapping, address lookup and direction services.
It checks whether the request also contains your company name, a site code or a staff member name.
It records the account, the device and the source address that made the request.
It removes internal facilities and marketing accounts that do this as part of their work.
Requests from external or unusual sources are grouped and sent to the security team as a lead.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital reception desk with a visitor book. Anyone can write a name and a room number. One visitor writes a name. Then they ask the receptionist for the home address of a consultant. They also ask for the staff car park layout. Nothing illegal has happened. But the receptionist remembers the conversation and writes a note. If the same person returns two days later, the pattern is obvious. This detection is that note, kept so a later pattern can be found.
takeaways: Physical information is reconnaissance too, and it enables attacks the network cannot see.
The important detail is who is looking and how often, not the individual search.
Feed these leads to your physical security team, not only to the network team.

objectives: Explain why physical location information is collected during the reconnaissance stage
Identify proxy, resolver and physical access telemetry that can reveal location research
Build a rule that pairs an organisation indicator with address or mapping terms
Recognise the internal teams whose normal work looks like this behaviour
Describe how location reconnaissance supports social engineering and physical intrusion
Escalate a credible lead to physical security and executive protection teams
dataSources: Secure web gateway logs containing the requested uniform resource locator and query string for mapping and address lookup services
Recursive domain name system resolver logs for mapping, geolocation and property record domains
Identity provider sign in and search activity records showing which account performed address or map queries
Physical access control system records for badge reads and visitor management sign ins at corporate sites
Facilities and site inventory listing public addresses, site codes and building names used as match terms
logic: The detection looks for a request that combines an organisation specific term with a location oriented destination or query. The location oriented side is a mapping, address lookup, directions or property record service, identified by host name or by the words in the query string. The organisation side is the company name, a site code, a building name or an employee name drawn from the site inventory. The fields that must be correlated are the resolved destination host, the full query string, the authenticated account, the device identifier and the source address. The malicious case is an unauthenticated or external source, a public egress address not used by staff, or a short burst that queries several different sites and executive names in sequence. The benign case is a facilities coordinator or marketing staff member looking up a public office address from a managed device during the working day, which is why account and source context, not the query alone, decides the alert.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Organisation Name Queried Against Mapping Or Address Lookup Service
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection_service:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'maps.google'
#       - 'openstreetmap.org'
#       - 'bing.com/maps'
#       - 'whitepages'
#   selection_org:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'acme-corp'
#       - 'building-west'
#   filter_internal:
#     src_ip|startswith:
#       - '10[.]10[.]0[.]'
#     group|contains: 'facilities'
#   condition: selection_service and selection_org and not filter_internal
# level: low
falsePositives: Facilities, reception and marketing staff looking up the public address or directions to a company site as part of their normal duties
Employees planning travel to a customer or partner office and searching for a nearby hotel or transport route
Recruiters and sales staff researching a company location before a meeting or an interview
Security teams performing authorised open source intelligence collection against the organisation's own public footprint
tuningNotes: Anchor the rule with a list of organisation terms that are unlikely to appear in ordinary web searches, such as site codes and building names, instead of the generic company name, and maintain that list with the facilities team so that it tracks office moves. Add filters for the accounts and device groups that legitimately do this work, keyed on the identity provider group rather than on a source address, because staff work from home. Scope the first release to external source addresses and to accounts outside the facilities and marketing groups. Narrowing to site codes costs you visibility into research using a street name or a postcode alone, so keep a lower severity rule that alerts when a single external source queries several of your public sites within one hour.
